title: The splashes at the laundry
hookLine: dirty water in her face at the washing tub, again and again, and the choice she makes about it
tomorrow: what can you give when you've got nothing big to give?

cards: Rain on a windshield. A sprinkler you didn't see coming. Somebody at the next sink who shakes their hands dry right at you.

Thérèse worked in the convent laundry, standing at a washing tub. The sister across from her was washing handkerchiefs, and every time she slapped one down, dirty water splashed up into Thérèse's face. Again.
And again. It is a small thing, and it is also every few seconds, for as long as the washing lasts. And her first instinct, she admits, was not a holy one.

teach.b: She wanted to step back and wipe her face, slowly and pointedly, so the sister would get the hint. Then she stopped.
Why refuse a gift handed out this freely? So she stayed where she was, and kept the struggle off her face. That was the hard part: not the water, the face.
Then she starts to smile at herself.
She says she tried to want the water, and ended up finding a taste for this new kind of sprinkling. Catholics hear the joke.
At some Masses the priest walks the aisle sprinkling the people with holy water, to an old chant from Psalm 50, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed."
The rite is called the Asperges, from the chant's first Latin word. Her washing tub became her sprinkling rite. She even promised herself she'd come back to that lucky spot.
Notice what she never does. She doesn't ask the sister to be careful. Nobody else notices.
The splash stays small, and so does the gift.
One honest limit: this is a story about splashes. Thérèse is showing how to take a small irritation, not how to stay quiet when someone is truly hurting you.
And here's one to tell a friend tonight: a saint's lesson on patience comes with a wet face and a joke about holy water.

how: At some Masses the priest sprinkles the people with holy water as a reminder of baptism, and Catholics often tell Thérèse's laundry story as an example of offering small annoyances quietly.

games.q: what does “the splashes at the laundry” mean?
o: extra washing a nun was given for breaking a rule
the holy water blessing given to nuns who work hard
dirty water Thérèse chose to take quietly, as a gift

games.q: the washing tub — tap the pairs.
p: wipe her face so she'd notice
thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop

s: offering it up means putting up with anything, even real harm
Thérèse's story is about splashes: small irritations, taken quietly. it isn't a rule to stay silent about harm.
Thérèse's first instinct was to wipe her face so the sister would notice
she admits it. then she chose to stay put.
Thérèse asked the sister to be more careful
she never said a word, and nobody else noticed.

games.q: two hours into a movie, the kid behind you keeps lightly bumping your seat. it's small, and the film is almost over. what does the washing tub suggest?
o: let this small one go quietly, as a little splash.
turn around and stare until the kid gets the hint.
move seats, loudly, so the parents see what happened.
games.why: Thérèse's first instinct was the pointed wipe, the stare. she let the small splash be small. (something harmful, or that won't stop, is a different story.)

practice: Wet your fingertips with cool water, or touch a damp cloth, and settle back into your seat. As the sit runs, feel the water drying on your skin, and let one small irritation from today ride along with it: received, not argued with.

wordCard.voice: The splashes at the laundry. Dirty water in the face, taken quietly, like a blessing nobody else saw.

orig.note: Latin for 'thou shalt sprinkle', the opening of the sprinkling chant from Psalm 50 in the Vulgate.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: a little splash, received quietly, can still be a gift. Dry off, and see you tomorrow.
